No elibrary.maff.gov.kh URL is visible on the scanned pages provided, so none is given here — confirm the source link if this file is later cross-checked against the online elibrary.
text: After cutting, rice must be threshed (បោកបែន, separating grain from the straw/panicle) and dried (សម្ងួត) before it is safe to store. The source describes a range of threshing methods from traditional to mechanized: beating bundles by hand or against a frame, trampling by draft animals or feet, a foot-pedal thresher (ម៉ាស៊ីនបោកបែនជើងទាត់), and a motorized mechanical thresher (ម៉ាស៊ីនបោកបែនម៉ូតូ/ម៉ាស៊ីនកិនស្រូវសម្រាប់បោកបែន). Traditional hand or animal threshing needs little equipment and works anywhere, but is slow, physically demanding, and can leave a higher share of unthreshed or damaged grain if not done carefully. Pedal and motorized threshers process far more paddy per hour with less manual effort and generally give cleaner threshing with less grain loss, but represent a cost (purchase or hire) and need reasonably dry bundles to work well. Whichever method is used, threshing should happen promptly after cutting rather than leaving cut or bundled rice standing in the field or in piles for extended periods, since delayed threshing is one of the loss points highlighted in the source's loss-by-stage breakdown. After threshing and basic cleaning (ការសម្អាត, removing straw, chaff, and foreign material), grain should be dried promptly — commonly by spreading it in a thin, even layer on mats or a hard clean surface to dry in the sun (ការហាលថ្ងៃ), turning periodically for even drying — down to a moisture level safe for storage. The source's storage-safety discussion points to roughly 13-14% moisture as the general target range for paddy going into storage (with milled rice needing similarly low moisture to resist mold and pests); grain left wetter than this for extended periods is far more prone to mold, insect buildup, and quality loss. Delayed drying after threshing — for example leaving damp grain piled up overnight while waiting for good weather — is flagged as a common cause of avoidable quality loss. (Note: moisture and capacity figures here are illustrative ranges from the source; actual safe-storage moisture can vary somewhat by storage duration, container type, and climate, so use a moisture meter where possible rather than judging by feel alone.)
